Identify target-gene variants and the numbers of HUMAN individuals carrying each
variant in this article's study. Read methods, results, tables, footnotes, and
article-bound supplements together. Extract three distinct fields:

animals, or the overall number screened for per-variant people. A multi-variant
cohort total cannot be copied onto each variant. Do not treat every case in a
disease-ascertained cohort as affected without applicable phenotype evidence.

current-study and cited prior-study cohorts, or overlapping patient lists.

quote or exact table header plus row, source locator, count role, basis, and scope.

valid; your job here is an independent reading, with all uncertainty retained.

# MAIN TEXT

## U-waves and T-wave peak to T-wave end intervals in patients with catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, effects of beta-blockers

### Abstract

Background Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT) is characterized by risk of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (pVT) and sudden death during stress. Experimental CPVT models show that delayed afterdepolarization (DAD)–induced triggered activity is the initiating mechanism of pVT, whereas an increase in transmural dispersion of repolarization (TDR) controls degeneration of pVT to ventricular fibrillation. U-wave and T-wave peak to T-wave end interval (TPE) are regarded as electrocardiographic counterparts of DAD and TDR, respectively. Objective We tested hypotheses that patients with CPVT might show abnormal U-waves and TPE intervals and that beta-blockers could suppress appearance of these repolarization abnormalities. Methods We reviewed Holter recordings from 19 CPVT patients with a RyR2 mutation (P2328S or V4653F) and from 19 healthy unaffected subjects to record U-waves and TPE intervals as well as to measure beta-blockers' effects on ventricular repolarization by use of an automated computerized program. Results The maximal U-wave to T-wave amplitude ratio was 0.8 ± 0.6 in CPVT patients and 0.4 ± 0.3 in unaffected subjects ( P = .009). Patients with most ventricular extrasystoles had a higher U-wave to T-wave amplitude ratio than those with fewest extrasystoles. Treatment with beta-blockers decreased U-wave amplitude at high heart rates. CPVT patients had longer TPE intervals than unaffected subjects at high heart rates, and beta-blocker treatment shortened their TPE intervals. Conclusion Present data support the hypothesis that U-waves associate with the DAD-triggered extrasystolic activity in CPVT patients. Patients with a RyR2 mutation show increased TPE at high heart rates. Beta-blocker treatment suppresses observed repolarization abnormalities in CPVT patients.

### Introduction

Mutations in the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2) gene underlie an autosomally dominantly inherited arrhythmia syndrome called catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT). 1 CPVT is characterized by exercise-related or stress-related ventricular tachycardia episodes in the absence of structural heart disease. 2 Without treatment, patients have syncopal events and a high probability of sudden cardiac death caused by malignant ventricular arrhythmias, with approximately 30% mortality by the age of 30 years. 2 Treatment with beta-blockers may prevent these cardiac events. 3 A clinical diagnosis is supported by the typical onset of ventricular arrhythmias during and fading of these arrhythmias after exercise or stress testing. As the work load and the heart rate increase, arrhythmias become more frequent and more complex until polymorphic or bidirectional ventricular tachycardia may occur. 4 In resting electrocardiogram (ECG), however, there is no known ECG marker of the syndrome. 4

Experimental studies suggest that delayed afterdepolarization (DAD)–induced triggered activity is the initiating mechanism of the typical polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (pVT) in CPVT patients. 5 In a clinical study, patients with RyR2 mutations showed late-appearing U-waves coinciding with DADs, 6 suggesting U-waves as potential ECG markers of arrhythmia vulnerability. Late-appearing U-waves were distinct from simultaneous double T-waves in the same patients. 6 Similar double T-waves or T-wave humps are typical in the long QT syndrome, and the terms T1 and T2 (instead of T and U) are recommended in cases with split T-waves. 7 High T2-waves are ECG counterparts for early afterdepolarizations (EADs) 8 which mediate triggered activity as the initiating arrhythmia mechanism in the long QT syndrome. 7 Although double T-waves were observed in RyR2 mutation patients, 6 the experimental data relating T2-waves to EADs and arrhythmia mechanism in CPVT patients are lacking. On the other hand, experimental studies with a RyR2 mutation model show that an increase in transmural dispersion of repolarization (TDR) is important for the degeneration of the initially slow pVT to ventricular fibrillation. 9 In clinical electrophysiology, the T-wave peak to T-wave end (TPE) interval serves as an ECG estimate of TDR. 10

Recently, Liu et al 11 showed that low-amplitude DADs are already present in unstimulated myocytes with mutant RyR2s, and beta-adrenergic stimulation enhances the development of DADs. In the clinic, however, it is unclear whether patients with RyR2 mutations show dynamic ECG ventricular repolarization abnormalities as compared with unaffected healthy subjects. We used ambulatory ECG recordings with detailed dynamic repolarization analyses 12,13 to detect these potential abnormalities. We tested the hypotheses that CPVT patients might show abnormal U-waves and abnormal TPE intervals and that beta-blockers could suppress the appearance of these repolarization abnormalities in RyR2-mutation patients.

### Methods

#### Study subjects

We studied 19 CPVT patients and 19 unaffected control subjects. For this study, we reviewed Finnish families with a known RyR2 mutation. Nineteen gene-positive patients coming from 2 affected families participated in the study protocol. Thus, a 24-h ECG recording was performed in each patient carrying 1 of 2 different RyR2 mutations (P2328S, n = 13, or V4653F, n = 6). Thirteen patients (68%) had either exercise-related syncope or cardiac arrest in their medical history ( Table 1 ). In the past history of the 2 families, the cumulative mortality by the age of 30 years was 31%. 2

All CPVT patients had normal findings on echocardiography, and at baseline electrolyte test, none showed electrolyte abnormalities. None of the patients were taking any medications known to affect the QT interval. The CPVT patients first performed a bicycle ergometer exercise test with continuous ECG recording. The heart rate at which ventricular bigeminy appeared was recorded. After the exercise test the 24-h ECG recording was started. Treatment with beta-adrenergic blocking agents was discontinued at least 5 drug half-lives before the exercise test until the study protocols were completed. After completing the tests, all 17 patients using regular beta-blocker medication continued the treatment. Two asymptomatic patients with no ventricular arrhythmias during exercise testing did not use beta-blocker medications. Twelve of 17 patients (P2328S, n = 6; V4653F, n = 6) repeated a second 24-h ECG recording while on a tolerable dose of a beta-blocker medication ( Table 1 ); 5 patients refused the second Holter recording.

For control subjects, we reviewed our database of genotyped unaffected healthy family members of patients with symptomatic long QT syndrome with available Holter recordings. We took the closest age match for each male patient and each female patient with a RyR2 mutation. No control subject took beta-blockers or any other medication known to affect cardiac repolarization.

Table 1 shows the ECG characteristics of the study subjects. All study subjects were in sinus rhythm, and none showed a bundle-branch block. Normal daily activities were encouraged during the recordings. The study complies with the Declaration of Helsinki. The Ethical Review Committee of the Department of Medicine, University of Helsinki, approved the study and informed consent was obtained from all participants.

#### Holter recordings and analyses

The 24-h ECG recordings were done using commercial tape recorders (model 8500; Marquette Electronics Inc., Milwaukee, WI). The tapes were initially analyzed with a Marquette 8000 Holter Analysis system (version 5.8 software) to label the QRS complexes to normal, ventricular extrasystoles, or aberrant complexes. The ECG data were then transferred to a personal computer for further analysis.

#### Measurement of the T1-waves, T2-waves, and U-waves and QT interval durations

We first reviewed the morphology of ventricular repolarization in the 24-h ECG recordings using the superimposed scan. When 2 or 3 distinct measurable positive deflections during the repolarization were present, the first peak was regarded as a T1-wave. The second peak was interpreted as a T2-wave if it separated from or merged with the T1-wave during the recording. 12 If the second peak in the time course remained separated from the T1-wave, possibly appearing and disappearing but never merging with the T1-wave, it was interpreted as a U-wave. See Figure 1 for the explanation of the terms used. A possibly occurring third peak, never merging into the T1-wave, was also regarded as a U-wave. Figure 2 shows a representative example with simultaneously occurring T1-waves, T2-waves, and U-waves. Note the ability of the T2-wave to merge occasionally with the T1-wave and occasionally with the U-wave, whereas the U-wave remains separated from the T-wave complex.

Samples with the highest T2-waves and U-wave amplitude and with the highest T2 to T1 amplitude ratios, as well as the highest U-wave to T-wave (T1 or T2, whichever was higher) amplitude ratios, were all printed on chart paper. We measured the maximal T2 to T1 amplitude ratios and corresponding U-wave to T-wave ratios manually from the ECG strips printed on chart paper at the speed of 50 mm/s and with the amplitude calibration of 0.1 mV/mm using modified lead V5. Both T1-waves and T2-waves as well as U-waves were required to be ≥0.1 mV in amplitude for the strip to be included in the measurements. We recorded the maximal values of the defined amplitude ratios as the mean of 5 consecutive beats for each individual if ≥1.1, otherwise we used the value of 1 as the individual maximum.

To measure the QT interval durations from the 24-h ECG recordings, we used a previously described method for determination of the QT intervals. 13 In this study, bifid T-waves showing a time interval of ≤0.15 s between the first peak (T1) and the later peak (T2) were calculated into the QT duration; otherwise, the later peak was not included into the QT duration. The TPE interval was measured from T1 to the end of QT interval, thus U-waves were not included in these measurements. We recorded diurnal median QT intervals at specified RR intervals determined at stable heart rates. 13 We also recorded median and maximal TPE intervals at specified heart rates. We calculated the median T-wave (T1) amplitude as well as median U-wave amplitude from corresponding values of ≥0.1 mV at specified heart rates. All analyses were done without the investigator knowing the genotypes or presence or absence of the beta-blocker medication. The baseline QT interval adjusted for heart rate (QTc) was measured in lead II from 12-lead ECGs using the Bazett formula.

#### Statistical analyses

Continuous variables are presented as mean ± SD. Differences in the normally distributed variables were assessed using the t test and the paired t test for dependent variables. Mann-Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed rank test were used as nonparametric tests when appropriate. Proportions were compared by χ 2 or Fisher exact tests as appropriate. All tests were 2-sided, and a probability value of P < .05 was considered statistically significant. SPSS version 14.0 (SPSS Inc, Chicago, IL) was used for data analysis.

### Results

#### QT and TPE intervals

The CPVT patient group showed a tendency to longer QTc in the baseline ECG as compared with the control patients ( Table 1 ). When compared at same heart rates during the 24-h recordings, the QT intervals were similar in both study groups (data not shown). Diurnal median TPE interval values were likewise similar in the study groups ( Table 2 ). In contrast, the patterns of the maximal TPE intervals were different between the study groups in that control subjects showed a longer maximal TPE interval at moderately high heart rates, whereas CPVT patients showed longer maximal TPE intervals at high heart rates ( Figure 3 ).

#### T2-waves and U-waves

The CPVT patients showed T-waves (T1) of lower amplitude than the unaffected subjects ( Figure 4 ). The T2-wave to T1-wave amplitude ratio of more than 1 was observed in 17 of 19 (89%) CPVT patients, and in 14 of 19 (74%) unaffected subjects. The maximal T2-wave to T1-wave amplitude ratio was 1.9 ± 0.7 (range 1 to 3.2) among CPVT patients and 1.4 ± 0.4 (range 1 to 2) in unaffected subjects ( P = .03).

Six of 19 (32%) CPVT patients and 1 of 19 (5%) unaffected subjects showed U-waves of higher amplitude than T-waves (T1 and T2) during 24-h recordings. Episodes with the U-wave higher than the T-wave typically lasted only a few seconds ( Figure 2 ). Separate U-waves with an amplitude higher than 0.1 mV were present in 18 CPVT patients (95%) and in 10 unaffected subjects (53%; P = .008). The amplitude of U-waves was highest at high heart rates in both study groups ( Figure 4 ). The maximal U-wave amplitude as well as the maximal U-wave to T-wave amplitude ratio was greater in the CPVT patient group ( Table 2 ). Maximal U-wave amplitude was 0.24 ± 0.09 mV among the 9 CPVT patients showing the most ventricular premature beats, whereas the corresponding value was 0.16 ± 0.04 mV among the 10 patients with the fewest extrasystoles ( P = .02). We observed ventricular premature beats on U-waves in 5 CPVT patients at high heart rates ( Figure 5 ).

The treatment with beta-blockers decreased the diurnal maximal T2-wave amplitudes ( Table 3 ). The maximal T2-wave to T1-wave amplitude ratio decreased from 2.1 ± 0.7 to 1.4 ± 0.5 ( P = .003), with each 11 patient out of the 12 exhibiting a baseline value of >1 showing a decrease. The median U-wave amplitude at heart rate of 120 beats/min was lower during the beta-blocker treatment ( Table 3 ).

### Discussion

#### Main findings

One novel finding of our research is that CPVT patients have abruptly emerging abnormalities in ventricular repolarization. CPVT patients had higher U-wave to T-wave and higher T2-wave to T1-wave amplitude ratios than healthy unaffected subjects. Patients with the highest U-waves showed more ventricular premature beats that temporally occurred on U-waves. At high heart rates, CPVT patients had longer TPE intervals than unaffected subjects. Treatment with beta-blockers showed apparently favorable effects by decreasing U-wave amplitude and maximal TPE intervals at high heart rates. Beta-blocker treatment decreased also the T2-wave to T1-wave amplitude ratio.

#### T2-waves and U-waves in CPVT patients, effects of beta-blockers

In accordance with previous reports, our CPVT patients showed normal T-waves in the baseline ECG. 2,3 During 24-h ECG recordings, however, CPVT patients occasionally showed double T-waves (with both T1 and T2) and U-waves simultaneously, as recently reported by Paavola et al 6 during a low dose of epinephrine infusion. Using an experimental model of type 2 long QT syndrome, Gbadebo et al 14 showed that the ratio of U-wave (T2 in the present study) to T-wave (T1 in the present study) amplitude could be used as an electrocardiographic counterpart of EAD in predicting the acute onset of torsades de pointes. In accordance with the experimental observation by Gbadebo et al, the T2-wave to T1-wave amplitude ratio correlated with the symptom history in patients with long QT syndrome types 1 and 2. 12 Systematic evaluation of the prevalence and behavior of T2-waves in patients with long Qt syndrome types 1 and 2.12 CPVT patients has not been presented earlier, however.

We observed high T2-wave to T1-wave amplitude ratios in CPVT patients. We also found that beta-blocker treatment decreased the T2 to T1 amplitude ratio in CPVT patients with type 1 long QT syndrome similarly as previously observed in patients. 15 The present findings suggest that patients with a RyR2 mutation are susceptible to the EAD-mediated arrhythmia mechanism, and beta-blocker treatment suppresses this mechanism.

We found separate U-waves with an amplitude higher than that of T-waves (T1 and T2) in one-third of CPVT patients. In clinical electrophysiology, separate U-waves have been considered to be of lower amplitude than T-waves, whereas late components of T-waves (T2-waves) may be very high in patients with long QT syndrome types 1 and 2. 12 Previously high-amplitude U-waves have been observed in patients with idiopathic ventricular tachycardia originating from the right ventricular outflow tract. 16 It is of interest that patients with Andersen-Tawil syndrome, resulting from mutations of the potassium channel KCNJ2 gene, show prominent U-waves in the baseline ECG. 17 The dynamics of the U-waves in patients with Andersen-Tawil syndrome have not yet been studied.

In this study, CPVT patients showing the greatest number of ventricular extrasystoles had the largest U-waves, U-waves were highest at elevated heart rates when the arrhythmias occur, and ventricular premature beats temporally occurred on U-waves. In harmony with a recent study by Paavola et al 6 in which CPVT patients showed prominent U-waves and ventricular extrasystoles coinciding with DADs in simultaneous monophasic action potential recordings, the present data support the hypothesis that in CPVT patients, U-waves can be used as a marker of DAD-triggered extrasystolic activity. Our observation that beta-blockers lowered the amplitude of U-waves suggests this as one of the possible mechanisms for the favorable effects of beta-blockers previously reported in CPVT patients.

Experimental studies ascribe the ionic background of EADs to reactivation of L-type I Ca or Na + /Ca 2+ exchange current 18 and the corresponding background of DADs to nonelectrically driven Ca 2+ events, depolarizing membrane potential during diastole by activating Na + /Ca 2+ exchange and Cl currents. 19 The presence of simultaneous T2-waves and U-waves as well as high T2 to T1 and high U-wave to T-wave amplitude ratios, representing clinical counterparts to EADs and DADs, respectively, in the same CPVT patients suggests that the 2 triggered activity mechanisms may be involved in the arrhythmogenesis associated with an inherited gain-of-function defect in RyR2 receptors. An EAD-mediated arrhythmia mechanism has not been experimentally shown in CPVT patients, however.

#### TPE intervals in CPVT patients, effects of beta-blockers

Using an experimental model of leaky RyR2 calcium release channel, Nam et al 9 suggested that increases in TDR underlie the degeneration of initially slow pVT to ventricular fibrillation in CPVT patients. In their experimental model, prolongation of TPE interval paralleled the increase in TDR during extrasystolic beats originating from epicardium. In CPVT patients, no data concerning the TPE interval have been reported previously, however. On the other hand, the TPE interval in abnormally conducted beats may not be an exact model of transmural dispersion of repolarization. 20 In this study, we observed that the behavior of the TPE interval was different between the study groups, with CPVT patients showing longer TPE intervals than unaffected subjects at high heart rates at which ventricular extrasystoles occurred. We observed also that treatment with beta-blockers shortened these maximal TPE values in CPVT patients. The finding is very similar to what we recently reported in patients with type 1 long QT syndrome. 16 Thus, the present results indicate that a part of beta-blockers' favorable effects in CPVT patients may be based on a decrease in the TDR.

#### Study limitations

We studied the behavior of ECG ventricular repolarization in a limited number of CPVT patients with 2 different RyR2 mutations. It remains unclear whether the observed repolarization abnormalities are typical of all CPVT patients or whether different RyR2 mutations yield different repolarization phenotypes. We could not analyze the association of the observed repolarization abnormalities with the symptom history because only a small number of CPVT patients were asymptomatic; thus, the usefulness of the presented measures in clinical arrhythmia risk evaluation in CPVT patients remains unknown. Because at high heart rates it is difficult to identify the U-wave due to encroachment of the U-wave on the following P-wave, 16 we limited the analysis of the U-wave amplitude up to a heart rate of 120 beats/min, which is well below the average heart rate at which ventricular extrasystoles appeared during the exercise test. For the same reason, the occurrence of ventricular premature beats on U-waves remains speculative ( Figure 5 ). Although our observations showed a decreased maximal T2-wave to T1-wave amplitude ratio and at high heart rates decreased U-wave amplitude as well as shortened maximal TPE intervals in CPVT patients during beta-blocker treatment, i.e., findings that all are expected to be favorable signs of diminished arrhythmia risk, the clinical significance of the present findings to predict the benefit of beta-blocker treatment in CPVT patients remains unclear until prospective follow-up data are available.

### T2-waves and U-waves in CPVT patients, effects of beta-blockers

In accordance with previous reports, our CPVT patients showed normal T-waves in the baseline ECG. 2,3 During 24-h ECG recordings, however, CPVT patients occasionally showed double T-waves (with both T1 and T2) and U-waves simultaneously, as recently reported by Paavola et al 6 during a low dose of epinephrine infusion. Using an experimental model of type 2 long QT syndrome, Gbadebo et al 14 showed that the ratio of U-wave (T2 in the present study) to T-wave (T1 in the present study) amplitude could be used as an electrocardiographic counterpart of EAD in predicting the acute onset of torsades de pointes. In accordance with the experimental observation by Gbadebo et al, the T2-wave to T1-wave amplitude ratio correlated with the symptom history in patients with long QT syndrome types 1 and 2. 12 Systematic evaluation of the prevalence and behavior of T2-waves in patients with long Qt syndrome types 1 and 2.12 CPVT patients has not been presented earlier, however.

We observed high T2-wave to T1-wave amplitude ratios in CPVT patients. We also found that beta-blocker treatment decreased the T2 to T1 amplitude ratio in CPVT patients with type 1 long QT syndrome similarly as previously observed in patients. 15 The present findings suggest that patients with a RyR2 mutation are susceptible to the EAD-mediated arrhythmia mechanism, and beta-blocker treatment suppresses this mechanism.

We found separate U-waves with an amplitude higher than that of T-waves (T1 and T2) in one-third of CPVT patients. In clinical electrophysiology, separate U-waves have been considered to be of lower amplitude than T-waves, whereas late components of T-waves (T2-waves) may be very high in patients with long QT syndrome types 1 and 2. 12 Previously high-amplitude U-waves have been observed in patients with idiopathic ventricular tachycardia originating from the right ventricular outflow tract. 16 It is of interest that patients with Andersen-Tawil syndrome, resulting from mutations of the potassium channel KCNJ2 gene, show prominent U-waves in the baseline ECG. 17 The dynamics of the U-waves in patients with Andersen-Tawil syndrome have not yet been studied.

In this study, CPVT patients showing the greatest number of ventricular extrasystoles had the largest U-waves, U-waves were highest at elevated heart rates when the arrhythmias occur, and ventricular premature beats temporally occurred on U-waves. In harmony with a recent study by Paavola et al 6 in which CPVT patients showed prominent U-waves and ventricular extrasystoles coinciding with DADs in simultaneous monophasic action potential recordings, the present data support the hypothesis that in CPVT patients, U-waves can be used as a marker of DAD-triggered extrasystolic activity. Our observation that beta-blockers lowered the amplitude of U-waves suggests this as one of the possible mechanisms for the favorable effects of beta-blockers previously reported in CPVT patients.

Experimental studies ascribe the ionic background of EADs to reactivation of L-type I Ca or Na + /Ca 2+ exchange current 18 and the corresponding background of DADs to nonelectrically driven Ca 2+ events, depolarizing membrane potential during diastole by activating Na + /Ca 2+ exchange and Cl currents. 19 The presence of simultaneous T2-waves and U-waves as well as high T2 to T1 and high U-wave to T-wave amplitude ratios, representing clinical counterparts to EADs and DADs, respectively, in the same CPVT patients suggests that the 2 triggered activity mechanisms may be involved in the arrhythmogenesis associated with an inherited gain-of-function defect in RyR2 receptors. An EAD-mediated arrhythmia mechanism has not been experimentally shown in CPVT patients, however.

### TPE intervals in CPVT patients, effects of beta-blockers

Using an experimental model of leaky RyR2 calcium release channel, Nam et al 9 suggested that increases in TDR underlie the degeneration of initially slow pVT to ventricular fibrillation in CPVT patients. In their experimental model, prolongation of TPE interval paralleled the increase in TDR during extrasystolic beats originating from epicardium. In CPVT patients, no data concerning the TPE interval have been reported previously, however. On the other hand, the TPE interval in abnormally conducted beats may not be an exact model of transmural dispersion of repolarization. 20 In this study, we observed that the behavior of the TPE interval was different between the study groups, with CPVT patients showing longer TPE intervals than unaffected subjects at high heart rates at which ventricular extrasystoles occurred. We observed also that treatment with beta-blockers shortened these maximal TPE values in CPVT patients. The finding is very similar to what we recently reported in patients with type 1 long QT syndrome. 16 Thus, the present results indicate that a part of beta-blockers' favorable effects in CPVT patients may be based on a decrease in the TDR.

### Study limitations

We studied the behavior of ECG ventricular repolarization in a limited number of CPVT patients with 2 different RyR2 mutations. It remains unclear whether the observed repolarization abnormalities are typical of all CPVT patients or whether different RyR2 mutations yield different repolarization phenotypes. We could not analyze the association of the observed repolarization abnormalities with the symptom history because only a small number of CPVT patients were asymptomatic; thus, the usefulness of the presented measures in clinical arrhythmia risk evaluation in CPVT patients remains unknown. Because at high heart rates it is difficult to identify the U-wave due to encroachment of the U-wave on the following P-wave, 16 we limited the analysis of the U-wave amplitude up to a heart rate of 120 beats/min, which is well below the average heart rate at which ventricular extrasystoles appeared during the exercise test. For the same reason, the occurrence of ventricular premature beats on U-waves remains speculative ( Figure 5 ). Although our observations showed a decreased maximal T2-wave to T1-wave amplitude ratio and at high heart rates decreased U-wave amplitude as well as shortened maximal TPE intervals in CPVT patients during beta-blocker treatment, i.e., findings that all are expected to be favorable signs of diminished arrhythmia risk, the clinical significance of the present findings to predict the benefit of beta-blocker treatment in CPVT patients remains unclear until prospective follow-up data are available.

### Conclusion

This study shows for the first time that CPVT patients carrying an inherited gain-of-function defect of RyR2 receptors show abruptly appearing and disappearing ECG ventricular repolarization abnormalities, and these repolarization changes attenuate with the use of beta-blockers. Similar DAD-mediated triggered activity mechanisms are believed to play an important role in the arrhythmogenesis associated with strong sympathetic stimulation, 21 heart failure, 22 and the occurrence of RyR2 mutations. 6 Our findings encourage using the presented approach in assessing the DAD-mediated arrhythmia mechanisms in the clinical evaluation of all of those patient groups.
